a: a proud man
t: A proud man or a scoffer?
p: The Greek warns against a proud man; the Hebrew against a scoffer, the mocker of Proverbs.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus agree
readings.orig: ὑπερηφάνῳ
readings.en: with a proud man
readings.plain: a proud man

readings.w: Hebrew: Cairo Genizah manuscript A (Cambridge, T-S 12.864), folio V recto, line 22 (Abegg's transcription)
readings.orig: וחובר אל לץ ילמד דרכו
readings.en: whoever joins a scoffer will learn his way
readings.plain: a scoffer

why: The Plain translates the Greek, the base text. The Hebrew "scoffer" (lets) is the word Proverbs uses for the mocker who will not take correction; the grandson chose a word for pride, perhaps because the rich and proud are the subject of the chapter.

a: for your fall walks right beside you
t: Walking with your fall, or with violent men?
p: The Greek warns that ruin walks beside you; the Hebrew says do not walk with violent men; the longer Greek adds a line.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ὅτι μετὰ τῆς πτώσεώς σου περιπατεῖς
readings.en: for you walk with your own fall
readings.plain: for your fall walks right beside you

readings.w: Hebrew: Cairo Genizah manuscript A (Cambridge, T-S 12.864), folio V verso, lines 7-8 (Abegg's transcription)
readings.orig: ואל תהלך עם אנשי חמס
readings.en: and do not walk with men of violence
readings.plain: and do not walk with men of violence

readings.w: Minuscule 248 (Vatican codex 346), as J. H. A. Hart prints it (1909, page image); Hart's commentary names 106 and 253 with it, with small differences; KJV "when thou hearest these things, awake in thy sleep"
readings.orig: ὅτι μετὰ τῆς πτώσεώς σου περιπατεῖς. ἀκούων ταῦτα ἐν ὕπνῳ σου γρηγόρησον πάσῃ ζωῇ.
readings.en: for you walk with your fall. Hearing these things in your sleep, keep awake all your life.
readings.plain: for your fall walks right beside you. / When you hear this in your sleep, keep awake all your life

why: The Plain follows Vaticanus. The Hebrew may be the older sense ("men of violence" is a common Hebrew phrase); the Greek of Vaticanus reads like a free rendering. The longer Greek line is not in Vaticanus, and Swete's notes record none in Sinaiticus or Alexandrinus. In Hart's text of 248 "all your life" ends this added line ("keep awake all your life"), with a full stop before "Love the Lord" (13:14); the Latin puts "all thy life" with the loving instead (Vulgate 13:18, "Omni vita tua dilige Deum"), and the KJV follows the Latin division.

a: [Love the Lord,
t: A verse found only in the longer text
p: Vaticanus has no line here. The longer Greek and the Latin have it, but they divide the words differently.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Swete's notes record no line in Sinaiticus or Alexandrinus either; the Hebrew of manuscript A has no such line (folio V verso, line 8, runs from 13:13 straight to 13:15)
readings.en: (no line)

readings.w: Minuscule 248 (Vatican codex 346), as J. H. A. Hart prints it (1909, page image), after the added line at the end of 13:13; Hart's commentary names 106 and 253 with it
readings.orig: ἀγάπα τὸν κύριον καὶ ἐπικαλοῦ αὐτὸν εἰς σωτηρίαν σου.
readings.en: love the Lord and call on him for your salvation
readings.plain: [Love the Lord,

readings.w: Latin Vulgate 13:18 "Omni vita tua dilige Deum, et invoca illum in salute tua" (Douay "Love God all thy life, and call upon him for thy salvation"); KJV 13:14 "Love the Lord all thy life"
readings.orig: Omni vita tua dilige Deum, et invoca illum in salute tua
readings.en: all your life love God, and call on him in your salvation
readings.plain: [Love the Lord all your life,

why: Every verse number needs a line, so the Plain gives this one in square brackets, translated from Hart's text of minuscule 248. The brackets show it is not in Codex Vaticanus, the base text. Hart prints a full stop after "all your life" (πάσῃ ζωῇ), which ends the added line of 13:13, so the Plain does not carry "all your life" into this verse; the Latin and the KJV put it here. Hart's commentary suggests that "all your life love" (πάσῃ ζωῇ ἀγάπα) was adapted from "every living thing loves" (πᾶν ζῷον ἀγαπᾷ) in 13:15. It is an addition of the longer text, not part of the grandson's translation.
b: Hart's commentary gives the longer reading as one addition at the end of 13:13: "hearing these things in your sleep, wake up ... love the Lord and call on him for your salvation" (minuscules 106, 248, 253). The Latin has the same two lines as its 13:17-18.

a: in the mouth of the ungodly
t: Godly or ungodly?
p: Vaticanus reads "godly"; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus read "ungodly," as the KJV does. The Plain departs from Vaticanus here.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἐν στόμασιν εὐσεβοῦς
readings.en: in the mouths of the godly
readings.plain: in the mouth of the godly

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Alexandrinus (A), as in Swete's notes; minuscule 248 as Hart prints it (page image); KJV "in the mouth of the ungodly"
readings.orig: ἀσεβοῦς
readings.en: of the ungodly
readings.plain: in the mouth of the ungodly

readings.w: Hebrew: Cairo Genizah manuscript A (Cambridge, T-S 12.864), folio V verso, lines 18-19 (Abegg's transcription)
readings.orig: ורע העוני על פי זדון
readings.en: and poverty is evil in the mouth (or: by the measure) of the insolent
readings.plain: in the mouth of the insolent

why: This is one of the few places where the Plain leaves Swete's Vaticanus. "Godly" makes poor sense: the couplet sets wealth without sin against poverty as the arrogant see it, and the Hebrew "insolent" supports Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus. The two Greek words differ only in their first letters (eusebous / asebous), an easy slip for a copyist. Hart prints "ungodly" (ἀσεβοῦς) in minuscule 248 as well (page image).

a: stung with grief over sin
t: Grief over sin, or many sins?
p: Vaticanus says "grief of sin"; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus "grief of sins"; minuscule 248 and the KJV "the multitude of sins."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ οὐ κατενύγη ἐν λύπῃ ἁμαρτίας
readings.en: and was not stung in grief of sin
readings.plain: stung with grief over sin

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Alexandrinus (A), as in Swete's notes
readings.orig: ἁμαρτιῶν
readings.en: of sins
readings.plain: stung with grief over sins

readings.w: Minuscule 248 (Vatican codex 346), as J. H. A. Hart prints it (1909, page image); KJV "is not pricked with the multitude of sins"
readings.orig: καὶ οὐ κατενύγη ἐν πλήθει ἁμαρτιῶν
readings.en: and was not stung in a multitude of sins
readings.plain: stung by a mass of sins

why: The Plain follows Vaticanus. "Grief" is the pain of conscience that the next verse goes on to describe; 248's "multitude" turns the line into a statement about how much a person has sinned.

a: who has not fallen away from his hope
t: His hope, or his hope in the Lord?
p: Minuscule 248 and the KJV add "in the Lord."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ ὃς οὐκ ἔπεσεν ἀπὸ τῆς ἐλπίδος αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and who did not fall from his hope
readings.plain: who has not fallen away from his hope

readings.w: Minuscule 248 (Vatican codex 346), as J. H. A. Hart prints it (1909, page image); in Hart's commentary also 106 and 253; KJV "from his hope in the Lord"
readings.orig: καὶ ὃς οὐκ ἔπεσεν ἀπὸ τῆς ἐλπίδος αὐτοῦ τῆς ἐπὶ Κύριον
readings.en: and who did not fall from his hope that is in the Lord
readings.plain: who has not fallen away from his hope in the Lord

why: The Plain follows Vaticanus. The addition names what the hope rests on; it does not change the sense.

a: he does it in a moment of forgetting
t: By forgetting, or unwillingly?
p: Vaticanus says he does good "in forgetfulness"; minuscule 248, followed by the KJV, says "unwillingly."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus agree
readings.orig: ἐν λήθῃ ποιεῖ
readings.en: he does it in forgetfulness
readings.plain: he does it in a moment of forgetting

readings.w: Minuscule 248 (Vatican codex 346), in J. H. A. Hart's edition (1909); KJV "he doeth it unwillingly"
readings.orig: οὐχ ἑκὼν ποιεῖ
readings.en: he does it not willingly
readings.plain: it is against his will

why: The Plain follows Vaticanus: the miser does a good deed only by a slip, when he forgets his own rule. Hart prints 248's "not willingly," which the KJV translates. The Hebrew manuscript A has no 14:7-8: folio V verso, line 26, runs from 14:6 straight to 14:9.

a: he goes short at his own table
t: A line only in the Hebrew
p: The Hebrew adds a contrasting couplet about the generous "good eye."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ ἐνλιπὴς ἐπὶ τῆς τραπέζης αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and lacking at his own table
readings.plain: he goes short at his own table

readings.w: Hebrew: Cairo Genizah manuscript A (Cambridge, T-S 12.864), folio V verso, line 28 (Abegg's transcription)
readings.orig: עין טובה מרבה הלחם ומעין יבש יזל מים על השלחן
readings.en: a good eye makes the bread plenty, and a dry spring will pour water on the table
readings.plain: he goes short at his own table. / A good eye makes bread plenty, / and a dry spring pours water on the table

why: The Plain translates the Greek. The Hebrew couplet looks like an added contrast (the generous eye against the grudging one); the Greek and the Latin do not have it.

a: bring the Lord the offerings he deserves
t: Offerings to the Lord, or "make yourself fat"?
p: The Greek speaks of offerings to the Lord; the Hebrew tells the student to enjoy his means. The two may come from one Hebrew word.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ προσφορὰς Κυρίῳ ἀξίως πρόσαγε
readings.en: and bring offerings to the Lord worthily
readings.plain: bring the Lord the offerings he deserves

readings.w: Hebrew: Cairo Genizah manuscript A, folio V verso, line 29 (T-S 12.864), to folio VI recto, line 1 (T-S 12.863) (Abegg's transcription)
readings.orig: ולאל ידך הדשן
readings.en: and as far as your hand can, make yourself fat (enjoy plenty)
readings.plain: as far as your hand can reach, enjoy plenty

why: The Plain translates the Greek. Hart (1909) suggests why the two differ: the Hebrew idiom le'el yadkha, "as your hand is able," begins with the letters of le'el, "to God," and the Greek took it that way, then supplied offerings. The Hebrew fits the context (14:11-16 is about enjoying one's goods), but the Greek is the text the churches received.
b: Offerings to God do fit Ben Sira's thought elsewhere (7:31; 32:6-10, where 32:10 says to honor the Lord "with a good eye"), so the Greek is not out of place even if it arose from a misreading.

a: treat yourself
t: Treat yourself, or make yourself holy?
p: Vaticanus says "beguile your soul" (cheer yourself up); a corrector of Sinaiticus and several later copies have "sanctify," which the KJV follows.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: ἀπάτησον τὴν ψυχήν σου
readings.en: beguile your soul (divert yourself)
readings.plain: treat yourself

readings.w: A later corrector of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵc.a), as in Swete's notes; minuscule 248 as Hart prints it (page image), and in Hart's commentary also 106, 253 and 296; KJV "sanctify thy soul"
readings.orig: ἁγίασον τὴν ψυχήν σου
readings.en: sanctify your soul
readings.plain: make your soul holy

readings.w: Latin Vulgate 14:16 "justifica animam tuam" (Douay "justify thy soul")
readings.orig: justifica animam tuam
readings.en: justify your soul
readings.plain: put your soul right

readings.w: Hebrew: Cairo Genizah manuscript A (Cambridge, T-S 12.863), folio VI recto, line 5 (Abegg's transcription)
readings.orig: ופניק נפשך
readings.en: and pamper yourself
readings.plain: pamper yourself

why: The Plain follows Vaticanus, which the Hebrew "pamper yourself" supports; Alexandrinus has a misspelled form of the same verb (ἀποτησον, in Swete's notes). Greek apataō usually means "deceive," but with "your soul" it means to divert or cheer yourself. "Sanctify" and the Latin "justify" read the line as a call to holiness instead.

a: whose thoughts dwell on Wisdom
t: Meditates on wisdom, or dies in wisdom?
p: Vaticanus, with Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus as first written, reads "will die in wisdom." A corrector of Sinaiticus, most later copies and the Hebrew read "meditates." The Plain departs from Vaticanus.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Swete's notes record no other reading for the first hand of Sinaiticus or for Alexandrinus
readings.orig: ὃς ἐν σοφίᾳ τελευτήσει
readings.en: who will die in wisdom
readings.plain: who dies in Wisdom

readings.w: A later corrector of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵc.a), as in Swete's notes; in Hart's commentary also minuscules 70, 106, 248 and 253 (Hart prints 248 as μελετήσει καλά, "will meditate on good things," page image); KJV "doth meditate good things in wisdom"
readings.orig: ὃς ἐν σοφίᾳ μελετήσει
readings.en: who will meditate on wisdom
readings.plain: whose thoughts dwell on Wisdom

readings.w: Hebrew: Cairo Genizah manuscript A (Cambridge, T-S 12.863), folio VI recto, line 9 (Abegg's transcription)
readings.orig: אשרי אנוש בחכמה יהגה
readings.en: happy is the man who meditates on wisdom
readings.plain: whose thoughts dwell on Wisdom

why: Here the Plain leaves Vaticanus. Its teleutēsei, "will die," differs from meletēsei, "will meditate," by a few letters and breaks the parallel with the second line ("reasons things out"). The Hebrew yehgeh, "meditates," confirms the corrector and the later copies. Hart's commentary reports a Latin text with "morietur" ("will die") followed by an added line, "and he that shall meditate in his justice," which keeps both readings; the Clementine Vulgate has "morabitur" ("will dwell") with the same added line (Vulgate 14:22).

a: the Lord will make it prosper
t: Who makes praise prosper?
p: The Greek says the Lord will prosper praise; the Hebrew says the one who masters wisdom will teach it.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ ὁ κύριος εὐοδώσει αὐτόν
readings.en: and the Lord will make it prosper
readings.plain: the Lord will make it prosper

readings.w: Hebrew: Cairo Genizah manuscript A (Cambridge, T-S 12.863), folio VI recto, line 21 (Abegg's transcription)
readings.orig: ומשל בה ילמדנה
readings.en: and the one who rules over it will teach it
readings.plain: the one who is master of it will teach it

why: The Plain translates the Greek. The Hebrew first line also differs: "In the mouth of a wise man praise is spoken." Both make the same point: praise belongs with wisdom, not with the sinner of 15:9.

a: for what he hates you are not to do
t: "You are not to do" or "he did not do"?
p: The Greek gives a command to the reader; the Hebrew says God himself did not do (or make) what he hates.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus agree
readings.orig: ἃ γὰρ ἐμίσησεν, οὐ ποιήσεις
readings.en: for the things he hated, you shall not do
readings.plain: for what he hates you are not to do

readings.w: Hebrew: Cairo Genizah manuscript A (Cambridge, T-S 12.863), folio VI recto, line 22 (Abegg's transcription)
readings.orig: כי את אשר שנא לא עשה
readings.en: for what he hates he did not do (or: make)
readings.plain: for what he hates he did not do

why: The Plain translates the Greek, the base text. Many modern translations follow the Hebrew here, which fits the argument better: God cannot be the cause of sin, because he does not do what he hates. The Hebrew of the first line also differs: "My transgression is from God." The Greek has "because of the Lord I fell away."

a: He himself sent me off course
t: "He led me astray" or "He made me so"?
p: Several later Greek copies read "he formed me" instead of "he led me astray," turning the excuse into "God made me this way."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus agree
readings.orig: Αὐτός με ἐπλάνησεν
readings.en: he himself led me astray
readings.plain: He himself sent me off course

readings.w: Minuscules 55, 106, 157, 248, 296 and 307, as listed in Hart's textual commentary (1909); Hart prints ἐπλάνησεν in his text of 248 and notes the manuscript's ἔπλασεν at the foot of the page (page image)
readings.orig: Αὐτός με ἔπλασεν
readings.en: he himself formed me
readings.plain: He himself made me this way

readings.w: Hebrew: Cairo Genizah manuscript A (Cambridge, T-S 12.863), folio VI recto, line 23 (Abegg's transcription)
readings.orig: הוא התקילני
readings.en: he himself made me stumble
readings.plain: He himself made me stumble

why: The Plain follows Vaticanus. "Formed me" (eplasen for eplanēsen) is an easy copying change, but it gives the excuse a sharper edge: if God shaped me with this nature, my sin is his doing. 15:14 answers exactly that: he made the human being free to choose.

a: left him in the hand of his own choice
t: A doubled line in the Hebrew: "his robber"
p: The Hebrew has two lines where the Greek has one: God put man "in the hand of his robber" and "of his yetser."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus agree
readings.orig: καὶ ἀφῆκεν αὐτὸν ἐν χειρὶ διαβουλίου αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and left him in the hand of his deliberation
readings.plain: left him in the hand of his own choice

readings.w: Hebrew: Cairo Genizah manuscript A (Cambridge, T-S 12.863), folio VI recto, line 25 (Abegg's transcription)
readings.orig: וישתיהו ביד חותפו ויתנהו ביד יצרו
readings.en: and put him in the hand of his robber, and gave him into the hand of his inclination (yetser)
readings.plain: put him in the hand of his robber / and gave him into the hand of his inclination

why: The Plain translates the Greek. Hart (1909) explains the Hebrew "robber" (chotfo, one who seizes) as an addition that interprets the yetser as the evil inclination that snatches a person away; the Greek and the Latin know only one line, and the extra line clashes with the argument that people are free.

a: acting faithfully is a matter of good will
t: A line only in the Hebrew: "If you trust in him, you will live"
p: The Hebrew adds a third line close to Habakkuk 2:4.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ πίστιν ποίησαι εὐδοκίας
readings.en: and to act faithfully is (a matter) of good will
readings.plain: acting faithfully is a matter of good will

readings.w: Hebrew: Cairo Genizah manuscript A (Cambridge, T-S 12.863), folio VI recto, lines 26-27 (Abegg's transcription)
readings.orig: ותבונה לעשות רצונו אם תאמין בו גם אתה תחיה
readings.en: and understanding to do his will. If you trust in him, you too will live
readings.plain: understanding is doing his will. / If you trust in him, you too will live

why: The Plain translates the Greek. Its last word, eudokias, "of good will (good pleasure)," does not say whose: the line may mean that faithfulness is your own free choice, or that it is what pleases God; the Plain keeps the Greek's openness. Hart (1909) suggests that the Greek "faith" (pistis) comes from a Hebrew word for faithfulness read where manuscript A has "understanding," and that the Hebrew third line ("if you trust in him, you too will live") grew from the same variant, recalling Habakkuk 2:4, "the righteous will live by his faithfulness." The Latin adds "He added his commandments and precepts" before this verse (Vulgate 15:15), and Luther quotes that line in his reply to Erasmus.

a: If you are willing, you will keep the commandments
t: "You will keep" or "to keep"?
p: Vaticanus has a promise, "you will keep the commandments"; some later copies and the KJV have an infinitive; the Latin adds "they will keep you."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; minuscule 248 as Hart prints it (page image)
readings.orig: ἐὰν θέλῃς, συντηρήσεις ἐντολάς
readings.en: if you wish, you will keep the commandments
readings.plain: If you are willing, you will keep the commandments

readings.w: Minuscules 55, 157, 253 and 254, as listed in Hart's textual commentary (1909); KJV "If thou wilt, to keep the commandments"
readings.orig: συντηρῆσαι ἐντολάς
readings.en: to keep the commandments
readings.plain: If you are willing to keep the commandments

readings.w: Latin Vulgate 15:16 "Si volueris mandata servare, conservabunt te" (Douay "If thou wilt keep the commandments ... they shall preserve thee")
readings.orig: Si volueris mandata servare, conservabunt te
readings.en: if you are willing to keep the commandments, they will keep you
readings.plain: If you are willing to keep the commandments, they will keep you safe

why: The Plain follows Vaticanus: the line promises that the willing person will keep the commandments, which is Ben Sira's point against the excuse of 15:11-12. The Latin's "they will keep you" is the form Luther quotes ("they shall preserve thee") in his reply to Erasmus.

a: no one has his leave to sin
t: Extra lines in the Hebrew and the Latin
p: The Hebrew and the Latin each add lines at the end of the chapter.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ οὐκ ἔδωκεν ἄνεσιν οὐδενὶ ἁμαρτάνειν
readings.en: and he gave no one relief (license) to sin
readings.plain: no one has his leave to sin

readings.w: Hebrew: Cairo Genizah manuscript A (Cambridge, T-S 12.863), folio VI verso, lines 1-2 (Abegg's transcription)
readings.orig: ולא החלים אנשי כזב ולא מרחם על עושה שוא ועל מגלה סוד
readings.en: and he did not strengthen men of falsehood; and he has no pity on one who does what is false, or on one who reveals a secret
readings.plain: he did not give strength to liars. / He has no pity on one who does what is false / or on one who tells a secret

why: The Plain translates the Greek. The Hebrew second and third lines look like added comments. The Vulgate adds a different line that belongs with 16:1 ("he does not desire a multitude of faithless and useless children").

a: do not count on their place
t: Their place, or their number?
p: Vaticanus says "their place"; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus say "their number," which the KJV follows.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: καὶ μὴ ἔπεχε ἐπὶ τὸν τόπον αὐτῶν
readings.en: and do not rely on their place
readings.plain: do not count on their place

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Alexandrinus (A), as in Swete's notes; minuscule 248 as Hart prints it (page image); KJV "neither respect their multitude"
readings.orig: καὶ μὴ ἔπεχε ἐπὶ τὸ πλῆθος αὐτῶν
readings.en: and do not rely on their number
readings.plain: do not count on their numbers

readings.w: Hebrew: Cairo Genizah manuscript A (Cambridge, T-S 12.863), folio VI verso, lines 4-5 (Abegg's transcription)
readings.orig: ואל תבטח בעקבותם
readings.en: and do not trust in their future (their "heels," what comes after them)
readings.plain: do not trust in what comes after them

why: The Plain follows Vaticanus. "Their place" probably means their standing or their lasting place in the land; "their number" fits 16:1-2. The Hebrew adds lines ("for they will have no good end"; "better one who does his will than a thousand"), and a corrector of Sinaiticus adds a long passage of his own. The KJV's "one that is just is better than a thousand" also reflects a longer text.

a: the giants of long ago
t: Giants or princes?
p: The Greek has "the ancient giants"; the Hebrew has "the princes of old."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus agree
readings.orig: τῶν ἀρχαίων γιγάντων

readings.plain: the giants of long ago

readings.w: Hebrew: Cairo Genizah manuscript A (Cambridge, T-S 12.863), folio VI verso, line 10 (Abegg's transcription)
readings.orig: לנסיכי קדם המורים עולם בגבורתם

readings.plain: the princes of old

a: who broke away from him in their strength
t: "In the strength of their folly"
p: Minuscule 248 and the KJV add "of their folly."

readings.orig: οἳ ἀπέστησαν τῇ ἰσχύι αὐτῶν

a: The Lord alone will be proven right.
t: "And there is no other besides him"
p: The longer Greek and the KJV read "the Lord alone is righteous, and there is no other besides him."

readings.orig: Κύριος μόνος δικαιωθήσεται
readings.en: the Lord alone will be justified
readings.plain: The Lord alone will be proven right.

why: The Plain follows Vaticanus. The longer Greek's added line echoes Isaiah 45:21 ("there is no other god besides me"); the Latin adds a different line.

a: [He steers the world with the span of his hand,
t: A verse missing from Vaticanus: the King of all
p: Vaticanus has no line here. The longer Greek has two couplets on God steering the world; all four lines go together.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Swete's notes record no line in Sinaiticus or Alexandrinus; the Vulgate lacks it
readings.en: (no line)

readings.w: Minuscule 248 (Vatican codex 346), in J. H. A. Hart's edition (1909), with minuscules 70 and 106; KJV
readings.orig: οἰακίζων τὸν κόσμον ἐν σπιθαμῇ χειρὸς αὐτοῦ, καὶ πάντα ὑπακούει τῷ θελήματι αὐτοῦ· αὐτὸς γὰρ βασιλεὺς πάντων ἐν κράτει αὐτοῦ διαστέλλων ἐν αὐτοῖς ἅγια ἀπὸ βεβήλων
readings.en: steering the world in the span of his hand, and all things obey his will; for he is king of all in his might, separating among them holy things from common
readings.plain: [He steers the world with the span of his hand,

why: Every verse number needs a line, so the Plain gives this one in square brackets, translated from Hart's text of 248. The picture of God steering (oiakizō, "to work the tiller") the world held in "the span of his hand" draws on Isaiah 40:12, and "setting apart the holy from the ordinary" is the priests' task in Leviticus 10:10.

a: He has allowed no one to tell his works in full
t: "No one" or "To whom?"
p: Vaticanus makes a statement, "he allowed no one"; minuscule 248 and the KJV ask "To whom has he given power?"

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus (corrector), Alexandrinus and Ephraemi spell the word οὐδενί (Swete's notes)
readings.orig: οὐθενὶ ἐξεποίησεν ἐξαγγεῖλαι τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ
readings.en: he allowed no one to declare his works
readings.plain: He has allowed no one to tell his works in full

readings.w: Minuscule 248 (Vatican codex 346), as J. H. A. Hart prints it (1909, page image); KJV "To whom hath he given power to declare his works?"
readings.orig: τίνι ἐξεποίησεν ἐξαγγεῖλαι τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ;
readings.en: to whom has he allowed (it) to declare his works?
readings.plain: To whom has he given the power to tell his works?

readings.w: Latin Vulgate 18:2 "Quis sufficit enarrare opera illius?" (Douay "Who is able to declare his works?")
readings.orig: Quis sufficit enarrare opera illius?
readings.en: who is able to tell his works?
readings.plain: Who is able to tell his works?

why: The Plain follows Vaticanus. The question and the statement say the same thing: no one can tell all God's works. The question form matches the next line, "who will track down all his great deeds?"

a: that is how few the years are within the day of eternity
t: A few years or a thousand?
p: Vaticanus says "a few years"; minuscule 248 and the KJV say "a thousand years."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus agree
readings.orig: οὕτως ὀλίγα ἔτη ἐν ἡμέρᾳ αἰῶνος
readings.en: so are a few years in the day of eternity
readings.plain: that is how few the years are within the day of eternity

readings.w: Minuscule 248 (Vatican codex 346), in J. H. A. Hart's edition (1909); KJV "so are a thousand years to the days of eternity"
readings.orig: οὕτως χίλια ἔτη ἐν ἡμέραις αἰῶνος
readings.en: so are a thousand years in the days of eternity
readings.plain: that is what a thousand years are within the days of eternity

why: The Plain follows Vaticanus. "A thousand years" looks like a change toward Psalm 90:4; it makes the comparison even stronger.

a: Do not let anything keep you from paying a vow when it is due,
t: Paying a vow, or praying always?
p: The Greek is about paying a vow on time. The Latin reads "praying always."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus agree
readings.orig: μὴ ἐμποδισθῇς τοῦ ἀποδοῦναι εὐχὴν εὐκαίρως
readings.en: do not be hindered from paying a vow in good time
readings.plain: Do not let anything keep you from paying a vow when it is due,

readings.w: Latin Vulgate 18:22 "Non impediaris orare semper" (Douay "Let nothing hinder thee from praying always")
readings.orig: Non impediaris orare semper
readings.en: do not be hindered from praying always
readings.plain: Do not let anything keep you from praying always,

why: The Plain translates the Greek. The Greek euchē means both "prayer" and "vow," and the Latin took it as prayer; the verb "pay back" (apodounai) shows that a vow is meant.

a: Get yourself ready before you make a vow,
t: Prepare yourself, or prepare your vow?
p: The Greek says "prepare yourself"; a corrector of Sinaiticus has "prepare your prayer (vow)."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.orig: πρὶν εὔξασθαι ἑτοίμασον σεαυτόν
readings.en: before praying (or vowing), prepare yourself
readings.plain: Get yourself ready before you make a vow,

readings.w: A later corrector of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵc.a), as in Swete's notes
readings.orig: πρὶν εὔξασθαί σε ἑτοίμασον τὴν εὐχήν σου
readings.en: before you pray (vow), prepare your prayer (vow)
readings.plain: Before you make a vow, get your vow ready,

why: The Plain follows Vaticanus. The corrector of Sinaiticus makes the vow itself the thing to prepare; the sense is the same either way: think before you promise God anything.

p: Minuscule 248 and the KJV add a contrasting line: "but a fool will not observe the time."

readings.w: Hebrew: Cairo Genizah manuscript C, folio V recto, lines 3-4 (Abegg's transcription; the last letter of "anything" is lost and restored in brackets)
readings.orig: אל תהי זולל וסובא ומאומ[ה] אין בכיס
readings.en: do not be a glutton and a drunkard, when there is nothing in the purse
readings.plain: while there is nothing in your purse, like a glutton and a drunkard

why: The Plain follows Vaticanus. The Hebrew of manuscript C uses the words of Deuteronomy 21:20 and Proverbs 23:20-21 for the glutton and the drunkard, which the grandson rendered with the Septuagint's verb for feasting (see the note). Kahana's edition (1912) prints the last word as bakkim, a misprint for bakkis, "in the purse," which the manuscript has.
